extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, economists, students of political economy, and general readers interested in public finance and colonial administration
extracted.subtask_description: 18th-century political-economy analysis of state bankruptcy, coinage debasement, taxation systems (land, stamp, customs, excise), colonial finance, paper money, and the practical effects of different fiscal arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: State bankruptcy should be fair, open, and avowed
rubrics_metrics.description: "When it becomes necessary for a state to declare itself bankrupt, in the same manner as when it becomes necessary for an individual to do so, a fair, open, and avowed bankruptcy, is always the measure which is both least dishonourable to the debtor, and least hurtful to the creditor."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open, avowed bankruptcy is morally and practically preferable to covert tricks (e.g., secretly debasing coin) because it minimises dishonour and harm to creditors; concealment is both easily detected and pernicious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Augmentation (direct raising of denomination) vs adulteration (mixing alloy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction: augmentation ("a direct raising of the denomination of the coin") is an open, avowed operation; adulteration (mixing alloy into the standard) is usually concealed and fraudulent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Augmentation renames smaller-weight pieces with the old denomination (open injustice); adulteration issues similar-looking coins of less intrinsic value (treacherous fraud) and, when discovered, excites greater public indignation and is more often reversed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Augmentation is open injustice but less rancorous
rubrics_metrics.description: "An augmentation, or a direct raising of the denomination of the coin, always is, and from its nature must be, an open and avowed operation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because it is open, augmentation tends to cause less popular fury and is less commonly reversed; it is still an injustice of 'open violence' but politically different from concealed debasement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adulteration (debasement) is treacherous fraud and provokes greater indignation
rubrics_metrics.description: "The adulteration of the standard... has generally been a concealed operation... an injustice of treacherous fraud. This latter operation, therefore, as soon as it has been discovered... has always excited much greater indignation than the former."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited (King John of France, English coin under Henry VIII) show adulteration is done secretly by mint officers and typically leads to strong public backlash and eventual restoration of fineness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberation of public revenue requires revenue augmentation or expense reduction
rubrics_metrics.description: "That the public revenue of Great Britain can never be completely liberated, or even that any considerable progress can ever be made towards that liberation... That liberation... can never be brought about, without either some very considerable augmentation of the public revenue, or some equally considerable reduction of the public expense."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy must focus on either markedly increasing revenue or substantially cutting public expenditure to free the public revenue from debt obligations; incremental tweaks are unlikely to suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tax reform: equalize land and house-rent taxes and alter customs/excise to augment revenue
rubrics_metrics.description: "A more equal land tax, a more equal tax upon the rent of houses, and such alterations in the present system of customs and excise as those which have been mentioned... might, perhaps, without increasing the burden of the greater part of the people, but only distributing the weight of it more equally upon the whole, produce a considerable augmentation of revenue."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Redistributive changes in tax incidence (more equality in land and house-rent taxation and streamlined customs/excise) can raise revenue while avoiding greater burdens on most people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extending taxation requires proportional political representation
rubrics_metrics.description: "By extending the British system of taxation to all the different provinces of the empire... this, however, could scarce, perhaps, be done, consistently with the principles of the British constitution, without admitting... a fair and equal representation of all those different provinces."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applying metropolitan taxes to colonies or provinces implies a political obligation to admit them to proportional representation (each province's representation bearing proportion to tax produce); absence of representation creates political obstacles and injustice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of stamp duties depends on similarity of legal instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: "Stamp duties, it is evident, might be levied without any variation, in all countries where the forms of law process, and the deeds by which property, both real and personal, is transferred, are the same, or nearly the same."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stamp duties are transferable across jurisdictions where legal forms are similar; administrative ease and uniformity make them broadly applicable in such contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excise laws must be adapted to local production and consumption
rubrics_metrics.description: "The excise is the only part of the British system of taxation, which would require to be varied in any respect, according as it was applied to the different provinces of the empire."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because consumption patterns differ (e.g., American fermented liquor made from molasses brewed at home), excise rules require local modification to avoid impractical enforcement or liberty infringements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid household-level excise enforcement on private families
rubrics_metrics.description: "To subject every private family to the odious visits and examination of the tax-gatherers... would be altogether inconsistent with liberty."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not enforce excise by intrusive inspections of private homes; instead tax materials, imports, or allow compounding schemes to respect personal liberty and practicality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative taxation methods for household-produced goods
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed alternatives: tax the material of production at manufacture, impose import duties into the consuming colony, allow each family to compound for consumption (by household size or demographic composition), or levy taxes centrally in the metropole (Sir Matthew Decker's proposal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose method based on practicality and liberty: material/import taxation avoids household inspections; compounding can be done by household composition; central levying can simplify administration for perishable domestic products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sugar, rum, and tobacco are appropriate subjects for taxation
rubrics_metrics.description: "Sugar, rum, and tobacco, are commodities which are nowhere necessaries of life... and which are, therefore, extremely proper subjects of taxation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such widely consumed non-necessities are good revenue sources; taxation can be implemented before leaving producer hands or via warehousing and controlled release mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warehouse taxation with deferred payment and duty-free export on security
rubrics_metrics.description: Tax these commodities "either before they go out of the hands of the manufacturer or grower; or... deposited in public warehouses... to remain there, under the joint custody of the owner and the revenue officer, till such time as they should be delivered out... the tax not to be advanced till such delivery. When delivered out for exportation, to go duty-free, upon proper security being given..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use bonded warehouses with joint custody and deferred taxation; enable duty-free exports on appropriate security to avoid taxing goods in transit and to simplify enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consolidate duties and apply excise enforcement to reduce smuggling
rubrics_metrics.description: "If the duties upon malt and malt liquors, were to be levied by a single duty upon malt, the opportunity of smuggling in the most important branch of the excise would be almost entirely taken away; and if the duties of customs... were confined to a few of the most general use and consumption, and if the levying of those duties were subjected to the excise laws, the opportunity of smuggling... would be very much diminished."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplifying and consolidating duties (e.g., single malt duty) and subsuming customs levying under excise mechanisms reduces incentives and opportunities for smuggling, especially in thinly inhabited areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper currency sufficient for domestic transactions in peacetime
rubrics_metrics.description: "The domestic business of every country... may, at least in peaceable times, be transacted by means of a paper currency, with nearly the same degree of conveniency as by gold and silver money."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paper money is a practical medium for domestic commerce; colonial governments can supply it, sometimes deriving revenue by lending it or issuing it in emergencies and later redeeming it at depreciated values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scarcity of metallic money often due to choice for productive capital
rubrics_metrics.description: "The present scarcity of gold and silver money in America, is not the effect of the poverty of that country... The scarcity of those metals, therefore, must be the effect of choice, and not of necessity."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Colonists prefer to invest surplus in active, productive stock rather than hold costly metallic money; this institutional preference explains low metallic circulation more than poverty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of metallic money in external trade depends on necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: "In the exterior commerce which the different colonies carry on with Great Britain, gold and silver are more or less employed, exactly in proportion as they are more or less necessary."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where balance of trade requires it, colonies pay in gold and silver; otherwise payments in commodities (e.g., tobacco, sugar) or bills of exchange often substitute for specie.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irregular colonial payments often caused by speculative over-expansion
rubrics_metrics.description: "The difficulty and irregularity of payment from the different colonies... have, upon this account, been, in general, more irregular and uncertain... [in proportion] to the quantity of uncultivated land which they contained; that is, to the greater or smaller temptation which the planters have been under of over-trading, or of undertaking the settlement and plantation of greater quantities of waste land than suited the extent of their capitals."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fiscal irregularity is linked to opportunities for speculation and over-extension (e.g., large uncultivated islands); well-settled, fully cultivated colonies show steadier returns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colonies can remit revenue by bills drawn on metropolitan merchants rather than specie exports
rubrics_metrics.description: "It might not, however, be necessary to remit any part of the American revenue in gold and silver. It might be remitted in bills drawn upon, and accepted by, particular merchants or companies in Great Britain... who would pay into the treasury the American revenue in money, after having themselves received the value of it in goods... and the whole business might frequently be transacted without exporting a single ounce of gold or silver from America."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use commercial credit instruments (bills of exchange) and merchant networks to transfer colonial revenue to the metropole, avoiding costly specie shipments and converting colonial produce into metropolitan cash via merchants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colonies' capacity justifies contribution to metropolitan public debt
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is not contrary to justice, that both Ireland and America should contribute towards the discharge of the public debt of Great Britain."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because colonies can produce surplus revenue and have capacity to remit value (in specie or bills), it is justifiable for them to bear part of the imperial debt service; practical arrangements must consider their economic circumstances.
